To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the recent increase in reported PR reserves and resources is based on the inclusion of upgraded PR concentrate in the reserves category, which is not a common mineral resource classification practice, and that the difference between PR ore, which is a raw mineral, and PR concentrate is not sufficiently noted in the PR scarcity literature, causing confusion and a high degree of error in various assessments of the PR scarcity problem.

(1) IFDC's simplified resource terminology does not meet the requirements for transparent, reliable and credible data, (2) the difference between raw PR ore, PR concentrate, and PR fertilizer should be noted in the literature to avoid confusion, and (3) the IFDC report is likely to present an inflated picture of PR reserves, in particular in Morocco.

(i) IFDC's simplified resource terminology does not comply with international best practice in mineral resource classification; (ii) the difference between PR ore (the mineral as extracted) and PR concentrate (the mineral after processing) is not adequately noted in the literature; (iii) the IFDC report most likely presents a significantly inflated picture of global PR reserves; and (iv) the statements in the literature that the available PR reserves and resources will last several thousands of year at current consumption rates are not supported
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quality of data on PR deposits, and we conclude that the data are not of sufficient quality for scientific or policy analysis.
the reliability of data on PR deposits, the implications of the IFDC classification for future research, and whether it is possible to reach agreement on a common classification for PR deposits.
the question of whether the recent increase in reported global PR reserves and resources, and the resulting change in the scarcity debate from resource scarcity to pollution, can be justified.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no evidence to suggest that the current PR reserves and resources will not last several hundreds of years at current rates of consumption, but that there is insufficient evidence to support the conclusion that the current reserves and resources will be adequate for several thousands of years.
the global PR resource base is large enough to last for several centuries, but that the global PR reserve base is not.
the global reserves and resources are currently not known with sufficient accuracy to allow a reliable estimate of their lifetime at current consumption rates, let alone at increased rates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IFDC report has not provided the scientific basis for the conclusion that there is a "sufficient" quantity of PR deposits available for future use.

the data on PR reserves are currently too uncertain to allow any conclusions about the future availability of the resource, while data on PR resources are likely inflated, in particular those reported for Morocco.
the current debate on PR scarcity is not well informed and that a significant number of analysts have been misled by the IFDC report.
